docs.title: Solution Design Document v1
docs.text:
Team: W18A-1 · Seminar: Wed 6 pm

Members: Kevin He, John Le, Ho Nam Wong, Sophia Lu, Lena Le

Roles today: Facilitators John Le and Lena Le, Timekeeper Sophia Lu, Scribe Kevin He, Challenger Ho Nam Wong

Problem statement v1: With ageing buildings and a lack of incentives to repair, property managers spend too much time coordinating severe maintenance repairs. This affects small and individual property managers, who spend most of their time on communication and maintenance admin. This bottleneck needs to change because it limits property managers' ability to keep residents satisfied and take on more properties.

How Might We: How might we build a product that makes communication about maintenance and tenant requests faster and easier to manage?

docs.title: 1. Concept and idea card
docs.text:
Selected concept: Dashboard and ticketing system with profiles Why: It covers all the issues in the problem statement while staying viable for user adoption. Rejected, and why: Automated Maintenance Assignment and Communication Forwarding and Rewording were rejected as standalone products. They were too wide in scope, and development could easily run into scope creep. Their strongest parts carry over as features of the selected concept: automated tradie recommendation and automated communication.

Concept Desirable Feasible Viable Total Dashboard and ticketing system with profiles 3 3 2 8 Automated Maintenance Assignment 2 2 2 6 Communication Forwarding and Rewording 3 2 1 6

Headline: myEST8 Description: A ticket ingestion and prioritisation platform for small property management agencies. Tenants report issues on the channels they already use: email, SMS or WhatsApp. An AI agent sorts each message, asks for photos through an upload link, checks them, and passes the issue to a property manager to confirm as a ticket. Tickets are ranked by urgency. For each job, myEST8 recommends tradies from their ratings and past quotes; the property manager requests quotes from 3–4 of them, compares at least two, and sends a work order. Property owners only approve when costs go over the property's limit, a shared calendar stops the agency double-booking tradies, and automated updates keep tenants, tradies and owners informed on their own channels. Problem statement: With ageing buildings and a lack of incentives to repair, property managers spend too much time coordinating severe maintenance repairs. This affects small and individual property managers, who spend most of their time on communication and maintenance admin. This bottleneck needs to change because it limits property managers' ability to keep residents satisfied and take on more properties. Users and stakeholders: Property managers (in agencies of 3–4), property owners, tradies, tenants, building managers (for common areas) Value: This solution matters because it frees up property managers' time to find and sign new property owners. It cuts the admin work that holds property management businesses back, and comparing at least two quotes per job helps keep maintenance costs down. Next steps and questions: - Verify viability through additional interviews. - Security and privacy review of the photo upload links and stored photo metadata (deferred for the MVP). - Check the urgent repair flow against NSW rules: tenants may arrange urgent repairs themselves only if they can't reach the landlord or agent, or the repair isn't done in a reasonable time. - Jev has been in limited early access since 15 September 2026. Confirm our access and usage limits will last the whole build. - Test whether photos uploaded from phone browsers keep their metadata.

docs.title: 2. Persona and user stories
docs.text:
Persona: Mohammed, 42, property manager Description: Runs a small property management business (~3 employees) and oversees about 100 properties within one suburb. Behaviours: - Uses AI a lot and often seeks guidance. - Spends a lot of time on admin work. - Communicates sporadically. - Checks email in the morning, then only occasionally.

Needs and goals: - Needs to grow the business by finding and talking to more clients. - Needs to keep tenants and property owners happy so they stay. - Goal: grow overall revenue and manage more properties. - Goal: reduce costs and expenses.

Evidence: Questionnaire

Epics: Capturing the full process for tradie discovery and quoting; Understanding the communication pathways; Creating wireframes for the solution; Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP)

# Epic User story Acceptance criteria Size 1 Capturing the full process for tradie discovery and quoting As a developer, I want a structured breakdown of each task and the endpoints connected to it, so that I can design an end-to-end process. 1 BPMN diagram and 1 design document for the process. M 2 Capturing the full process for tradie discovery and quoting As the BA/Scrum Master, I want to take the requirements from this process and break them down into tickets, so that the developers have tasks that work towards impact. 5 developer tickets created; 1 documentation submission. M 3 Capturing the full process for tradie discovery and quoting As the Product Owner, I want a tracker that maps tickets to user requirements, so that I can monitor progress towards business impact. 1 ticket progress tracker the Product Owner can view. L 4 Understanding the communication pathways As a developer, I want a map of every channel tenants, tradies and property owners use to contact the property manager, so that I know which channels the intake agent must support. 1 communication pathway map covering email, SMS and WhatsApp. S 5 Creating wireframes for the solution As a designer, I want wireframes of the main processes, so that we can check the flow with users before building it. Process wireframes in Figma, reviewed by the team (scope TBD). M 6 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want a guide to connect our email, SMS and WhatsApp, so that I can set myEST8 up without technical help. The guide connects all 3 channels and explains how to create any the agency doesn't have. M 7 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a tenant, I want to report an issue on the channel I already use and send photos through a link, so that I don't have to download an app or create an account. Messages on email, SMS and WhatsApp reach the agent; a new issue gets an upload link; uploaded photos attach to the maintenance request. L 8 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want each reported issue checked automatically before I confirm it, so that I only spend time on genuine issues. Each maintenance request shows its photo metadata and image-match results; confirming creates a ticket; rejecting tells the tenant why. M 9 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want tickets ranked by urgency, so that I deal with the most severe repairs first. Every issue is ranked Urgent, High or Routine; urgent issues get the urgent repair reminder; the dashboard sorts tickets by urgency, then by submission time. M 10 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want recommended tradies for each job and at least two quotes side by side, so that I can choose the best option in one place. 3–4 recommended tradies per job; quote requests sent in one click; at least 2 quotes compared before a work order can be sent. L 11 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property owner, I want to approve repairs only when they go over my limit, so that I keep control of big costs without being asked about small jobs. Approval is requested only when the repair cost would exceed the property's max repair cost; the YES/NO reply is recorded. M 12 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want to see when tradies are already booked by my colleagues, so that we don't double-book the same tradie. The shared calendar shows every scheduled job; new times are suggested when a tradie or tenant asks to reschedule. L 13 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want automatic updates sent on each person's own channel, so that I don't have to relay messages myself. Updates are sent at each status change, on the channel last used within 24 hours, otherwise by SMS or email. M 14 Building the core maintenance request workflow (MVP) As a property manager, I want to rate each tradie after a job, so that recommendations improve over time. The property manager gives a 1–5 rating; the tenant is asked "Was it fixed properly?"; both show on the tradie's profile. S

docs.title: 3. User flow
docs.text:
Tenant flow: 1. Message the agency on the channel they already use: email, SMS or WhatsApp. 2. If the issue is urgent, receive a reminder that tenants arrange urgent repairs themselves, using the property's nominated tradies where possible, and can claim up to $1,000 back from the property owner. Send the receipt (a photo or PDF) to the agency; the property manager checks it and forwards it to the owner. The flow ends here for urgent repairs. 3. Otherwise, answer a few guided questions from the agent and upload photos through the link it sends. 4. Receive a confirmation when the property manager confirms the issue as a ticket, or the reason if it's rejected. 5. Follow progress through status updates and the progress tracker. 6. Confirm the visit time, or ask for another one. 7. Let the tradie in, then answer "Was it fixed properly?" (1–5).

Property manager flow: 1. Set up the agency in the onboarding guide: connect email, SMS and WhatsApp, then add properties (with max repair cost, tenants, owner and nominated tradies) and existing tradies (with a starting rating). 2. Review maintenance requests with their automatic check results, and confirm or reject each one. Confirming creates a ticket, ranked by urgency on the dashboard. 3. Check the trade proposed for the ticket's first job, and add any further jobs. 4. For each job, choose 3–4 recommended tradies and send them quote requests. 5. Confirm the price and time read from each quote, then choose one once at least two are in. 6. If the repair cost would go over the property's max repair cost, wait for the owner's approval. 7. Send the work order with a time slot when the tradie is free on the shared calendar, and accept a suggested new time if the tradie or tenant asks to move it. 8. Rate the tradie when the job is done, and close the ticket once all its jobs are done.

Tradie flow: 1. Receive a quote request by SMS, email or WhatsApp. 2. Reply with a price and proposed time, as a message or a PDF quote. 3. If chosen, receive a work order with the visit time, and reply to ask for a different time if needed. 4. Do the job and reply to say it's done.

Property owner flow: 1. Receive an approval request when a ticket's repair cost would go over the property's max repair cost. It shows the full repair cost. 2. Reply YES or NO. A reminder follows after 24 hours. 3. Receive updates as the work goes ahead. 4. For urgent repairs the tenant arranged, receive the tenant's receipt once the property manager has checked and forwarded it (copied in), and reimburse the tenant up to $1,000.

docs.title: 4. Prioritised feature list
docs.text:
Core features (MVP): 1. Channel connections and onboarding guide: the agency connects its email, SMS and WhatsApp in an onboarding guide. If it doesn't have one of these channels, the guide walks the property manager through creating it. 2. AI intake agent: reads every message on the connected channels, works out who sent it, and sorts it into a new issue, an update on an existing ticket, a common area issue, or other. 3. Photo upload and verification: for a new issue, the agent sends the tenant an upload link by SMS or WhatsApp. Photos are checked automatically (photo metadata, and whether the image matches the description) before a property manager confirms the maintenance request, which creates the ticket. 4. Urgency ranking: every issue is ranked Urgent, High or Routine. Urgent repairs go back to the tenant to arrange; tickets are sorted so the most severe repairs are handled first. 5. Profiles: for properties (max repair cost, tenants, owner, nominated tradies, frequent issues), tenants and tradies (trades, ratings, quote history). 6. Tradie recommendation: for each job, myEST8 recommends tradies based on their myEST8 and Google ratings and their previous quotes. 7. Quote requests and comparison: the property manager sends quote requests to 3–4 recommended tradies and needs at least 2 quotes, compared side by side, before sending a work order. 8. Owner approval: the property owner approves when a ticket's repair cost would go over the property's max repair cost. 9. Shared calendar and scheduling: every scheduled job across the agency in one calendar, showing when each tradie is free, with suggested times when a visit needs to move. 10. Automated updates: status updates go to tenants, tradies and owners on the right channel at each step. 11. Ratings: after each job, the property manager rates the tradie and the tenant answers one question, which feeds the tradie's profile. 12. Progress tracker: a visual timeline of each ticket for the tenant and the property manager.

The MVP is a web app that also works in mobile browsers, built over 4 weeks.

Secondary features (after the 4-week MVP):

# Feature Notes 13 FAQ page Answers common tenant questions. 14 FAQ-powered chatbot Adapts its answers from the FAQ content, cutting repeat questions to the property manager. 15 Tradie sign-up Tradie accounts. Valuable for many features, but the MVP keeps every tradie on their existing channels. 16 Tradie calendar Tradies share their own availability. Requires tradie sign-up; the shared agency calendar covers part of this in the MVP. 17 Direct tenant–tradie connection Tenants and tradies coordinate visits directly. 18 Tenant check-ins The platform checks in on tenants periodically. 19 Regular tenant checks Tenants upload images and do regular checks to catch issues early. 20 Weekly quests and tenant score Small weekly tasks for tenants. The tenant score counts only verified tenant-caused damage and recorded lease breaches, never message volume, and stays inside the agency. 21 Voice communication Tenants can report and discuss issues by voice.

docs.title: 5. Data and logic
docs.text:
Collected: - From tenants: messages on email, SMS or WhatsApp, photos through the upload link (with any metadata), answers to the agent's guided questions, and a 1–5 answer to "Was it fixed properly?" after each job. - From tradies: quotes (price and proposed time) as free-text replies or PDFs, requests to change a visit time, and confirmation that a job is done. - From property owners: YES/NO replies to approval requests. - From property managers: channel connections, profile details, confirmations of maintenance requests, quote and work order decisions, and a 1–5 tradie rating after each job. - From Google: each tradie's overall Google rating, where they have a listing.

Stored: - Property profiles: address, property owner, current tenants, max repair cost, nominated tradies, building manager contact (strata properties), frequent issues and ticket history. - Tenant profiles: contact details, channels used, ticket history. - Tradie profiles: contact details, trades, myEST8 rating, Google rating, quote history, scheduled jobs. - Maintenance requests and tickets: description, photos, check results, urgency, status, jobs, and a log of every message. - Jobs: trade, quote requests, quotes, work order, scheduled time.

Presented: - Property manager dashboard: maintenance requests and their check results waiting for confirmation; tickets ranked by urgency; recommended tradies for each job; a side-by-side quote comparison; the shared calendar; the progress tracker; and an inbox for "other" and unknown-sender messages. - Tenant: replies and status updates on their own channel, the photo upload page and the progress tracker. - Tradie: quote requests, work orders and visit times on their own channel. - Property owner: approval requests showing the full repair cost, and updates on their own channel.

Logic rules: 1. Message handling: the agent matches each sender to a stored tenant, tradie or owner by phone number or email. Unknown senders go to the property manager's inbox; linking one to a person saves the number for next time. The message is then sorted: - New issue: goes through verification (rule 2). - Update on an existing ticket: attached to that ticket, including duplicate reports from housemates. - Common area issue: forwarded to the building manager, and the tenant is told it has been passed on. - Other: goes to the property manager's inbox untouched. 2. Verification: the agent asks a few guided questions and sends an upload link by SMS or WhatsApp. Each photo gets two automatic checks: its metadata, which is flagged only if it contradicts the report (taken before the tenancy began or well before the report, or far from the property; missing metadata doesn't count against it), and whether the image matches the description. The issue is then a maintenance request. A property manager confirms it, which creates the ticket, or rejects it, and the tenant is told why. 3. Urgency: each issue is ranked Urgent, High or Routine. Anything threatening safety, the structure, security or an essential service (e.g. gas leak, flooding, dangerous electrical fault, no hot water) is Urgent: the agent reminds the tenant that they arrange urgent repairs themselves, using the property's nominated tradies where possible, and can claim up to $1,000 back from the property owner. When the tenant sends the receipt, it becomes a Reimbursement Request: the property manager checks it and forwards it to the owner (copied in as a third party), then marks it reimbursed once the owner has paid. Damage that will worsen if left (e.g. a slow leak) is High; everything else is Routine. Tickets are sorted by urgency, then by submission time. 4. Trades: the trade for the ticket's first job is proposed automatically from a fixed list (plumbing, electrical, carpentry, roofing, appliances, locksmith, pest control, general handyman). The property manager can change it and add more jobs. 5. Tradie recommendation: for each job, recommend tradies with that trade: nominated tradies first, then ranked by a weighted blend of their myEST8 rating, Google rating, job fit (how closely their past work matches this job, judged by Jev) and previous quotes. The ratings and job fit are shown side by side, not combined. A tradie who isn't on Google keeps the starting rating the property manager gave them. 6. Quotes: the property manager sends quote requests to 3–4 recommended tradies. The agent reads the price and proposed time from each reply, and the property manager confirms them. Tradies who don't reply get a reminder after 48 hours; after 72 hours the property manager is prompted to invite more. At least 2 quotes are needed before a work order, unless the property manager records a reason for going ahead with one. 7. Owner approval: if approving a quote would take the ticket's repair cost over the property's max repair cost, the property owner must approve that quote. The request shows the full repair cost, and the owner replies YES or NO. The owner gets a reminder after 24 hours, and the property manager is alerted after 48. Quotes already approved stay approved. 8. Work orders and scheduling: the property manager sends a work order with a time slot (2 hours by default, adjustable) when the tradie is free in the shared calendar. The agent sends the slot to the tradie and the tenant, and either can ask for another time. Suggested new times are free for the tradie and fit the availability the tenant gave. 9. Choosing the channel: within 24 hours of a person's last message, reply on the channel they used. Otherwise send by SMS, or by email if there's no mobile number. 10. Ratings: when a job is done, the property manager rates the tradie 1–5 and the tenant is asked "Was it fixed properly?" (1–5). Both feed the tradie's myEST8 rating used in rule 5.

docs.title: 6. Platform shortlist
docs.text:
Platform Handles well Trade-off Our skill (1–3) GitHub Repository hosting and change tracking Merge conflicts, and a learning curve for anyone new to Git 2 VS Code Code editing, extensions and built-in Git integration Only an editor: hosting and deployment need other tools TBC Figma Process wireframes Wireframes only; prototypes aren't functional TBC Canva Quick visuals and presentation slides Limited for interactive wireframes TBC Twilio SMS, WhatsApp and (through SendGrid) inbound email from one provider The WhatsApp sandbox only allows 3 preset templates for messages we send first; real WhatsApp numbers need Meta verification TBC Jev (TypeSafe AI) Fast, typed classification decisions: message type, urgency, trade Text and JSON input only, can't write replies, limited early access TBC Claude Haiku (Anthropic) Composes outbound emails and messages, and each request's one-line Summary, from the ticket's facts Can invent details unless it's constrained to given facts; a cost per call TBC

Preferred: One web app that works in mobile browsers, built with GitHub and VS Code, using Twilio for the messaging channels, Jev for classification and Claude Haiku for composing messages. Figma is used only for process wireframes (TBD). Reason: Twilio covers all three channels with one integration. Jev returns typed decisions quickly and cheaply, which suits sorting every incoming message. A single app with internal modules keeps a 4-week build manageable for a team of 5.

As built (November 2026)

The channel providers changed during the build. Twilio could not be used: its trial can't send custom text, and our Australian regulatory bundle was rejected. SendGrid's free plan had also been retired. myEST8 now uses textbee for SMS, Resend for email and Meta's WhatsApp Cloud API for WhatsApp. It is built with Hono + Postgres (Supabase) on Vercel, with Jev classifying and Claude Haiku composing as planned. See Implementation and the Implementation Report.

docs.text:
This page walks through the steps for working on this repository with Git. The site is published from main; day-to-day work happens on dev.

To maintain control of changes @Kevin He and @John Le have been assigned as the reviewers of merge requests.

All changes that are pushed to dev will not be viewable in the docs website or in Github until either Kevin or John approve.

Our Github repo has three branches, main, dev and gh-pages. The first two are the only ones for acutal work gh-pages is only for hosting our documents.

docs.text:
All changes being made should be communicated in the group chat but in case something is being missed, make sure to frequently checkout before starting development.

Use the following commands for daily work:

git checkout dev
git pull origin dev          # get teammates' latest work

# ...edit files...

git status                   # see what changed
git add .                    # stage changes
git commit -m "Describe what you changed"
git push origin dev

Tip

Pull before you start working and before you push. It avoids most merge conflicts.

If you are adding any documentation made by an agent, please use the open preview using either Ctrl+K, V. Or the following UI button.

docs.title: Adding documentation (Lena, Sophia and the rest of the team)
docs.text:
You only ever work on dev. You never need to touch main or gh-pages.

  1. Switch to dev and get the latest work:

    git checkout dev
git pull origin dev

  2. Add or edit your Markdown files under docs-site/docs/. For a new page, also add it to nav: in docs-site/mkdocs.yml, otherwise the build fails. Use lowercase kebab-case file names and start each page with one # Title.

  3. For images, put them in docs-site/docs/Images/ and link them relative to your page, e.g. ![Alt text](Images/my-image.png).

  4. Check the build passes:

    cd docs-site
mkdocs build --strict

  5. Commit and push straight to dev:

    git add .
git commit -m "Add <what you added>"
git pull origin dev     # pick up anyone else's pushes first
git push origin dev

  6. When your work is ready to be published, tell Kevin or John. They open the pull request from dev into main and review it.

If git push is rejected, someone else pushed first. Run git pull origin dev and push again.

docs.title: Impact Delivery Report
docs.text: This report sets out the business impact myEST8 is designed to deliver, how the delivered MVP maps to it, and how we will measure it. myEST8 hasn't been used by a real Agency yet, so the impact figures here are projections built on stated assumptions. They will be checked against what Property Managers tell us in UAT (5–9 November 2026) and replaced with their numbers.

docs.title: 1. The problem we set out to solve
docs.text:
With ageing buildings and a lack of incentives to repair, property managers spend too much time coordinating severe maintenance repairs. This affects small and individual property managers, who spend most of their time on communication and maintenance admin. This bottleneck needs to change because it limits property managers' ability to keep residents satisfied and take on more properties.

The evidence behind it (full detail on Market Research and Problem Statement Refinement):

  • Workload: 66% of property managers describe their workload as busy or far too busy, and 29% intend to leave the industry (MRI, via Real Estate Business).
  • Capacity is shrinking: properties per manager fell from 122 to 116 between 2019 and 2023 (Macquarie Real Estate Benchmarking Report 2023).
  • Repairs are common and slow: 50% of renters live in homes needing repairs (UNSW Rights at Risk, 2025), and 38% of landlords had a tenant wait longer than is reasonable for a repair in the past year (Finder, 2025).
  • Coordination is manual: requests arrive through many channels and are tracked, prioritised and chased by hand, and tradie discovery relies on personal lists and word of mouth.

docs.title: 2. How the MVP delivers the impact
docs.text:
Each impact the design promised maps to features that are now built and running in production.

Intended impact Delivered by Who benefits Less time on communication The AI intake agent asks the follow-up questions, collects photos and writes the Summary. Automatic updates go out at every status change on each person's own channel. Property Manager Less time chasing Quote Requests in one click, automatic reminders (48 h for quotes, 24 h for Owner approvals, 24 h for visit offers) and alerts only when someone hasn't responded Property Manager Decisions, not admin The Dashboard shows only what needs the Property Manager's decision: confirm a request, choose a Firm Quote, or handle a stalled item. Everything else moves on its own. Property Manager, Agency principal Lower and more defensible repair costs At least two Firm Quotes compared side by side, recommendations weighted by rating, job fit and price, and Owner approval only above the Max Repair Cost Property Owner Faster, more transparent repairs for Tenants Report on any channel with no app or account, a live progress tracker, and visit times the Tenant picks Tenant Fewer wasted call-outs Photo and metadata checks before confirmation, and Site Inspections booked only when the Tradie asks for one Owner, Agency Correct handling of urgent repairs Urgent issues go straight to the Tenant with the Nominated Tradie and the $1,000 reimbursement process, which the Property Manager checks before forwarding Tenant, Owner, Agency (compliance) Capacity to grow Hours freed from admin can go to winning and serving more Owners (see §3) Agency principal

docs.title: 3. Projected time savings
docs.text:
Approach. For one repair, add up the Property Manager's coordination touches today and compare them with the touches left once myEST8 handles the routine ones. The minute values below are assumptions for illustration. UAT question 4 ("How do you handle repairs today, and how long does a typical repair take you?") will replace them.

Coordination step Today (manual), assumed With myEST8 What the Property Manager still does Take the report, ask follow-up questions, get photos 15 min 2 min Reads the Summary and confirms Find tradies and request quotes 15 min 2 min Ticks the recommended Tradies Chase and compare quotes 15 min 3 min Chooses a Firm Quote Get Owner approval (when over the limit) 10 min 0–1 min Nothing, unless the Owner doesn't reply Book the visit between Tradie and Tenant 15 min 1 min Nothing, unless asked to override Status updates to Tenant and Owner, close-out 10 min 1 min Rates the Tradie Total per repair ~80 min ~10 min

Illustrative Agency. Take the persona's portfolio of about 100 Properties per Property Manager, and assume 2 non-urgent repairs per Property per year:

  • 200 repairs × ~70 minutes saved ≈ 230 hours a year per Property Manager, or about 4.5 hours a week.
  • At the benchmark of about 116 Properties per manager, that is roughly the time needed to take on more Properties, which is the growth the problem statement says is being blocked. The exact number is for UAT testers to confirm or correct.

Projection, not a measurement

These figures depend entirely on the assumed minutes and repair volume. We'll report the UAT-derived version in §6 and say plainly if it comes out lower.

docs.title: 7. Risks to the impact
docs.text: Risk Effect on impact Mitigation Change resistance: people keep the processes they know Low adoption, so no time is saved Tenants, Tradies and Owners need no new app or account. Onboarding is a guided wizard, and spreadsheet import brings in existing records. AI misclassification (wrong Urgency or Trade) Rework, or an urgent issue handled late Low-confidence messages go to the Inbox. Every Maintenance Request is confirmed by a person. AI-written text is labelled. SMS regulation and provider limits The channel tenants use most is capped Email and WhatsApp keep working. The paid per-Agency SMS code is ready once approved. Privacy of Tenant data and photos Loss of trust; legal exposure Made-up data only for now, encrypted credentials and backups, and a security review planned before real data Fit with existing property management software Double entry reduces the time saved Spreadsheet import now; PMS integration prioritised by UAT feedback

docs.title: 8. Conclusion
docs.text: The MVP delivers every capability the design said was needed to cut a Property Manager's maintenance admin: intake, checking, quoting, approval, booking and updates now run on their own, and the Property Manager makes the decisions. The projected saving is large, about 4.5 hours a week for a manager with 100 Properties. It is still a projection until UAT confirms the baseline. The next step is to replace the assumptions in §3 with testers' own numbers and report the result here.

docs.title: 4. Decisions that changed during the build
docs.text:
The plan left three decisions open: the web framework, database and hosting; the vision model; and the quote-reading model. Several other decisions had to be revisited once real providers were tried. Each change is recorded as an ADR in the repository.

Area Planned Built Why it changed Framework, database, hosting Open Hono + Postgres (Supabase) on Vercel Hono runs unchanged on Node and on serverless. Postgres gives the transactions and locking needed when several Property Managers act at once. Everything fits free tiers. SMS Twilio textbee (Android phone gateway) Twilio's trial can't send custom text, and Twilio rejected our Australian regulatory bundle (22 Oct), so we couldn't get a number at all. The per-Agency Twilio code is kept but switched off (ADR 0005 → 0013). Email Twilio SendGrid Inbound Parse Resend with an inbound subdomain SendGrid's free plan was retired in May 2025. Gmail OAuth was tried next, but its tokens expire about every 7 days in Testing mode (ADR 0004 → 0006). WhatsApp Twilio sandbox Meta Cloud API, one server number Twilio was only a paid layer over Meta's API. The first version sent a verification code to the server's own number, which Meta refuses, so it was redesigned to connect without a code (ADR 0019). Classification Jev Jev, with Claude Haiku as fallback Jev suits typed judgments with probabilities. Haiku covers outages (ADR 0011). Writing messages Fixed templates only Haiku composes emails, with templates as fallback Template emails read as robotic. Code-checked composition keeps every fact exact (ADR 0008 → 0011). Guided questions Four questions, one at a time Haiku extracts what the Tenant already said, then asks once for the rest, at most twice Tenants were asked things they had already answered ("last night the sink broke" already says where and when) (ADR 0014) Quoting One quote step Estimate → optional Site Inspection → Firm Quote, per Tradie Australian tradies quote in stages, and an estimate isn't binding. A Firm Quote is now always required (ADR 0007 → 0009 → 0016). Scheduling Property Manager picks the time Tradie offers up to three times, Tenant picks Removes a round of phone tag. The Property Manager can still override (ADR 0015). Tradie ranking Strict tie-breaks on ratings Weighted blend including AI job fit Decimal ratings rarely tie, so Google rating and price never counted, and nothing looked at the Job itself (ADR 0016). Urgent Repair receipts Auto-forwarded to the Owner Property Manager checks, then forwards Unchecked files would have gone to Owners under the Agency's name (ADR 0010) Geocoding Google Nominatim + Photon Google Geocoding needs billing enabled. The OpenStreetMap services are free and match the map tiles (ADR 0012).

docs.title: 5. Challenges and how we handled them
docs.text:
1. Australian SMS regulation. This was the biggest risk. Real Australian SMS needs identity-verified numbers, and a student project couldn't get one through Twilio. textbee routes texts through a real SIM, at the cost of one shared number and the free-tier limits (50 texts a day, 300 a month). The Twilio code stays in place in case a bundle is approved later.
  2. Serverless background work. Vercel's free plan has no long-running process and only daily cron. We run the worker after every webhook and ping a cron route every 5 minutes from GitHub Actions. Tasks are claimed atomically and retried after 10 minutes if a run dies.
  3. Latency. Pages make several queries in a row. With the function in the default US region and the database in Seoul, every page took seconds. Moving the function to icn1, next to the database, fixed it.
  4. Keeping AI output trustworthy. Free-form model output can drop or invent an amount or a link. Composition is therefore checked by code against the template's facts and falls back to the template. AI text is labelled ✦✦ in the interface. Profile wording is written by code, never by a model.
  5. Testing without real providers. Every external service is behind a port with a mock, so the whole workflow (including two Property Managers acting at the same moment) is tested on real Postgres with a fake clock, with no secrets needed.
  6. Safe production releases. A university project has no staging. We added a strict dev → master release flow, additive-only migrations, post-deploy smoke tests, a one-click rollback workflow and weekly encrypted backups.

docs.title: 6. Delivery process
docs.text:
• Branching: feature branch → PR into dev, reviewed with CI green → release PR dev → master, which deploys. CI rejects PRs into master unless they come from dev or a hotfix/ branch.
  • Decisions were recorded as ADRs when they were made, and domain terms were kept in CONTEXT.md so code, interface and documentation use the same words (Maintenance Request, Ticket, Job, Firm Quote, Max Repair Cost…).
  • Issues were tracked as markdown files under .scratch/<feature>/, with triage labels.
  • AI-assisted development: coding agents worked on separate git worktrees under the same review and CI rules as human contributors. Agents open PRs but never merge to master.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
This page describes myEST8 as it was built and as it runs in production today. The plan it started from is on the Implementation Plan page. Where the build moved away from that plan, the reason is on the Implementation Report page.

  • Live app: https://myest8.vercel.app (production, deployed from master)
  • Source code: https://github.com/SweetTooth05/myEST8
  • Status: feature-complete MVP, in User Acceptance Testing (see UAT Testing)

docs.title: 1. What myEST8 does
docs.text:
myEST8 is a maintenance desk for small property management Agencies (3–4 Property Managers). Tenants report repairs on the channels they already use. myEST8 does the back-and-forth that normally fills a Property Manager's day: follow-up questions, photos, quotes, owner approval, booking and updates. The Property Manager steps in only to make decisions.

The end-to-end workflow:

  1. Report. A Tenant texts or emails the Agency, for example "the tap under the kitchen sink keeps dripping".
  2. Intake. The AI agent matches the sender to a Tenant and classifies the message (new issue, update, Common Area issue or other). It sets the Urgency (Urgent / High / Routine) and the Trade. It pulls out any details the Tenant already gave and asks only for the ones still missing, in a single message. Then it sends a no-login photo upload link.
  3. Check. Each photo is checked against its metadata (EXIF date and location) and against the description. Claude Haiku writes a one-line Summary, and the request waits on the Dashboard as a Maintenance Request.
  4. Confirm. The Property Manager reads the Summary, photos and checks, edits anything if needed, and confirms. That creates a numbered Ticket, and the Tenant gets a link to a progress tracker.
  5. Urgent Repairs never become Tickets. The Tenant is told to arrange the repair with the Property's Nominated Tradie and can claim up to $1,000 back. Their receipt becomes a Reimbursement Request, which the Property Manager checks and forwards to the Owner.
  6. Quote. myEST8 recommends Tradies for the Job and sends Quote Requests. Each Tradie gives an Estimate on a no-login quote page, says whether they need a Site Inspection, and then gives a Firm Quote. Firm Quotes are compared side by side.
  7. Approve. If the chosen quote would take the Ticket's Repair Cost over the Property's Max Repair Cost, the Owner is asked to reply YES or NO. Reminders go out at 24 h, and the Property Manager is alerted at 48 h.
  8. Book. The chosen Tradie offers a preferred visit time plus up to two more. The Tenant picks one and the Work Order goes out already confirmed. Either side can ask for another time.
  9. Close. The Tradie reports the Job done and the Tenant is asked "Was it fixed properly?". The Property Manager rates the Tradie, and both ratings feed future recommendations.

Only Property Managers have accounts. Tenants, Tradies and Property Owners never sign up. They use SMS, email or WhatsApp, plus a few single-purpose no-login links: photo upload, receipt upload, quote page, visit picker and progress tracker.

Additions not in the original design, driven by testing and feedback:

  • AI follow-up drafts. The Property Manager types a rough note, presses Draft with AI, edits the draft and sends it. Every AI-written message is marked ✦✦ ("Written by AI").
  • Approvals page: everything waiting on an Owner, with the amount and how long it has been waiting.
  • Archive of closed Tickets, and a Dashboard "Next 7 days" view.
  • Team management: invite or remove a Property Manager and edit the Agency.
  • Shared contact addresses: several people in one household can share a mobile or email. A message from a shared address is read as the person the Agency most recently asked.

The secondary features from the design (FAQ, chatbot, Tradie sign-up, Tenant check-ins, quests, voice) remain out of scope for the MVP.

docs.title: 3. Architecture
docs.text:
myEST8 is one app with internal modules, not microservices (ADR 0001). It is a TypeScript server built on Hono and renders HTML pages on the server. JavaScript is added only where a page needs it, such as the map, the upload page and in-place editing.

                 SMS (textbee)   Email (Resend)   WhatsApp (Meta)
                        │              │                │
                        └──── signed webhooks ──────────┘
                                       │
   Property Manager ──HTTPS──▶  Hono app (api/index.ts on Vercel)
   Tenant / Tradie no-login links ─▶   │
                                       ├── intake ──── Jev (classify) / Claude Haiku (extract, summarise)
                                       ├── tickets
                                       ├── quotes ───── Jev (job fit), Google Places (ratings)
                                       ├── scheduling
                                       ├── notifications ── Claude Haiku (compose) → template fallback
                                       ├── profiles / imports
                                       └── worker (background tasks: reminders, judgments, sends)
                                       │
                         Supabase Postgres  +  Supabase Storage (photos, receipts, PDFs)

docs.title: Modules (src/)
docs.text:
Module Responsibility intake.ts Sender matching, classification, guided questions, photo requests, Urgent Repairs tickets.ts Maintenance Requests, Tickets, Jobs, status timeline quotes.ts Tradie ranking, Quote Requests, Estimates, Site Inspections, Firm Quotes, Owner approval scheduling.ts Work Orders, visit offers, rescheduling, the shared calendar notifications.ts, templates.ts, composing.ts Choosing the channel, message templates, AI composition with fact checks profiles.ts, profile-reads.ts, imports.ts People and Properties, profile reads, spreadsheet import onboarding.ts, channel-verification.ts Sign-up, the welcome wizard, connecting Channels worker.ts Background task queue: reminders, AI judgments and delivery retries ports.ts + adapters/ One interface per external service, each with a real adapter and an in-process mock web/pages/ 30 server-rendered pages (Dashboard, Dispatch, Schedule, Approvals, Profiles, Ticket, Settings, …)

Ports and adapters. Every external service sits behind a port: classifier, summariser, composer, image matcher, quote reader, Places, geocoder, messenger and file storage. Each port has a real adapter and a mock. That is how the same code runs as the offline demo, in the test suite and in production. In production the app refuses to start if any required service is still mocked.

Background work. Vercel has no long-running process. The worker therefore runs straight after every webhook or upload, and a cron route (/api/cron/worker) drains anything due every 5 minutes. Tasks are claimed atomically, so two runs never take the same task. A task whose run died is retried after 10 minutes.

Data. Postgres has 17 additive migrations under supabase/migrations/. Row-level security is on with no policies, so Supabase's public API can read nothing. The app does its own per-Agency authorisation. Writes take a per-schema advisory lock, so a check made inside a transaction ("is this Job still choosing a Quote?") still holds when it writes.

docs.title: 5. AI in myEST8
docs.text:
The design rule is each model does the job it suits, and code owns the facts.

  • Jev classifies what comes in. Each incoming message becomes a set of typed questions with fixed answers: kind of message, what it relates to, Urgency, Trade, update type and the Owner's yes or no. Jev answers them all in one pass, with a probability for each answer. Below a confidence threshold, the message goes to the Inbox rather than being acted on. Jev also scores job fit (how closely a Tradie's past work matches this repair, on four levels) and judges each Maintenance Request once for the Tenant's profile read.
  • Claude Haiku writes what goes out. It writes the one-line Summary, composes outbound emails and drafts follow-ups, and it pulls the guided details (where, since when, getting worse, availability) out of a Tenant's free text.
  • Guardrails:
    • Haiku gets the facts as structured data, and a Tenant's own words are passed as untrusted data, never as instructions.
    • Code extracts every amount, date, link, phone number and button line from the template, and Haiku's draft is sent only if it contains all of them word for word and adds none.
    • Otherwise, or if Haiku is slow (8 s) or down, the fixed template is sent. Sending never depends on a model.
    • SMS, WhatsApp and verification messages are always template text.
    • Profile sentences are written by code from counts, never by a model, so a model is never the thing that says a Tenant caused damage.
  • Not chosen yet: a vision model for the photo-to-description match, and a model for reading prices out of PDF quotes. Both are defined as gateway contracts (image-matcher.ts, quote-reader.ts), and the Property Manager confirms every result. Tradies type their quotes on the no-login quote page, so PDF reading isn't on the critical path.

docs.title: 6. Security and privacy measures
docs.text:
• Passwords are hashed. Sign-in errors don't reveal whether an email exists. State-changing requests have same-origin checks.
  • All provider webhooks are signature-checked: textbee HMAC-SHA256, Meta X-Hub-Signature-256, Resend and Twilio signatures. An unknown or bad signature gets the same 403.
  • No-login links use unguessable per-item tokens and are rate limited. Opening a link never changes anything; a button press does.
  • Stored third-party credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM.
  • Database backups are piped straight into age encryption, so no plaintext dump exists.
  • Only made-up data is used. The Supabase project is in an Asia-Pacific region.

The no-login pages have not had an independent security review yet. That is listed under known limitations in the Implementation Report.

docs.title: Feature Description and Technology Usage
docs.text: This section covers the core and secondary features and the technologies used to implement them. The MVP is a single web app that also works in mobile browsers, built over 4 weeks. Domain terms such as maintenance request, ticket, job and max repair cost are defined in CONTEXT.md, and the key decisions are recorded in docs/adr/.

docs.title: Feature List
docs.text:
Core features (MVP): 1. Channel connections and onboarding guide: the agency connects its email, SMS and WhatsApp in an onboarding guide. If it doesn't have one of these channels, the guide walks the property manager through creating it. 2. AI intake agent: reads every message on the connected channels, works out who sent it, and sorts it into a new issue, an update on an existing ticket, a common area issue, or other. 3. Photo upload and verification: for a new issue, the agent sends the tenant an upload link by SMS or WhatsApp. Photos are checked automatically (photo metadata, and whether the image matches the description) before a property manager confirms the maintenance request, which creates the ticket. 4. Urgency ranking: every issue is ranked Urgent, High or Routine. Urgent repairs go back to the tenant to arrange; tickets are sorted so the most severe repairs are handled first. 5. Profiles: for properties (max repair cost, tenants, owner, nominated tradies, frequent issues), tenants and tradies (trades, ratings, quote history). 6. Tradie recommendation: for each job, myEST8 recommends tradies based on their myEST8 and Google ratings and their previous quotes. 7. Quote requests and comparison: the property manager sends quote requests to 3–4 recommended tradies and needs at least 2 quotes, compared side by side, before sending a work order. 8. Owner approval: the property owner approves when a ticket's repair cost would go over the property's max repair cost. 9. Shared calendar and scheduling: every scheduled job across the agency in one calendar, showing when each tradie is free, with suggested times when a visit needs to move. 10. Automated updates: status updates go to tenants, tradies and owners on the right channel at each step. 11. Ratings: after each job, the property manager rates the tradie and the tenant answers one question, which feeds the tradie's profile. 12. Progress tracker: a visual timeline of each ticket for the tenant and the property manager.

Secondary features (after the 4-week MVP):

# Feature Notes 13 FAQ page Answers common tenant questions. 14 FAQ-powered chatbot Adapts its answers from the FAQ content, cutting repeat questions to the property manager. 15 Tradie sign-up Tradie accounts. Valuable for many features, but the MVP keeps every tradie on their existing channels. 16 Tradie calendar Tradies share their own availability. Requires tradie sign-up; the shared agency calendar covers part of this in the MVP. 17 Direct tenant–tradie connection Tenants and tradies coordinate visits directly. 18 Tenant check-ins The platform checks in on tenants periodically. 19 Regular tenant checks Tenants upload images and do regular checks to catch issues early. 20 Weekly quests and tenant score Small weekly tasks for tenants. The tenant score counts only verified tenant-caused damage and recorded lease breaches, never message volume, and stays inside the agency. 21 Voice communication Tenants can report and discuss issues by voice.

docs.title: Data and logic
docs.text:
Collected: - From tenants: messages on email, SMS or WhatsApp, photos through the upload link (with any metadata), answers to the agent's guided questions, and a 1–5 answer to "Was it fixed properly?" after each job. - From tradies: quotes (price and proposed time) as free-text replies or PDFs, requests to change a visit time, and confirmation that a job is done. - From property owners: YES/NO replies to approval requests. - From property managers: channel connections, profile details, confirmations of maintenance requests, quote and work order decisions, and a 1–5 tradie rating after each job. - From Google: each tradie's overall Google rating, where they have a listing.

Stored: - Property profiles: address, property owner, current tenants, max repair cost, nominated tradies, building manager contact (strata properties), frequent issues and ticket history. - Tenant profiles: contact details, channels used, ticket history. - Tradie profiles: contact details, trades, myEST8 rating, Google rating, quote history, scheduled jobs. - Maintenance requests and tickets: description, photos, check results, urgency, status, jobs, and a log of every message. - Jobs: trade, quote requests, quotes, work order, scheduled time.

Presented: - Property manager dashboard: maintenance requests and their check results waiting for confirmation; tickets ranked by urgency; recommended tradies for each job; a side-by-side quote comparison; the shared calendar; the progress tracker; and an inbox for "other" and unknown-sender messages. - Tenant: replies and status updates on their own channel, the photo upload page and the progress tracker. - Tradie: quote requests, work orders and visit times on their own channel. - Property owner: approval requests showing the full repair cost, and updates on their own channel.

Logic rules: 1. Message handling: the agent matches each sender to a stored tenant, tradie or owner by phone number or email. Unknown senders go to the property manager's inbox; linking one to a person saves the number for next time. The message is then sorted: - New issue: goes through verification (rule 2). - Update on an existing ticket: attached to that ticket, including duplicate reports from housemates. - Common area issue: forwarded to the building manager, and the tenant is told it has been passed on. - Other: goes to the property manager's inbox untouched. 2. Verification: the agent asks a few guided questions and sends an upload link by SMS or WhatsApp. Each photo gets two automatic checks: its metadata, which is flagged only if it contradicts the report (taken before the tenancy began or well before the report, or far from the property; missing metadata doesn't count against it), and whether the image matches the description. The issue is then a maintenance request. A property manager confirms it, which creates the ticket, or rejects it, and the tenant is told why. 3. Urgency: each issue is ranked Urgent, High or Routine. Anything threatening safety, the structure, security or an essential service (e.g. gas leak, flooding, dangerous electrical fault, no hot water) is Urgent: the agent reminds the tenant that they arrange urgent repairs themselves, using the property's nominated tradies where possible, and can claim up to $1,000 back from the property owner. When the tenant sends the receipt, it becomes a Reimbursement Request: the property manager checks it and forwards it to the owner (copied in as a third party), then marks it reimbursed once the owner has paid. Damage that will worsen if left (e.g. a slow leak) is High; everything else is Routine. Tickets are sorted by urgency, then by submission time. 4. Trades: the trade for the ticket's first job is proposed automatically from a fixed list (plumbing, electrical, carpentry, roofing, appliances, locksmith, pest control, general handyman). The property manager can change it and add more jobs. 5. Tradie recommendation: for each job, recommend tradies with that trade: nominated tradies first, then ranked by a weighted blend of their myEST8 rating, Google rating, job fit (how closely their past work matches this job, judged by Jev) and previous quotes. The ratings and job fit are shown side by side, not combined. A tradie who isn't on Google keeps the starting rating the property manager gave them. 6. Quotes: the property manager sends quote requests to 3–4 recommended tradies. The agent reads the price and proposed time from each reply, and the property manager confirms them. Tradies who don't reply get a reminder after 48 hours; after 72 hours the property manager is prompted to invite more. At least 2 quotes are needed before a work order, unless the property manager records a reason for going ahead with one. 7. Owner approval: if approving a quote would take the ticket's repair cost over the property's max repair cost, the property owner must approve that quote. The request shows the full repair cost, and the owner replies YES or NO. The owner gets a reminder after 24 hours, and the property manager is alerted after 48. Quotes already approved stay approved. 8. Work orders and scheduling: the property manager sends a work order with a time slot (2 hours by default, adjustable) when the tradie is free in the shared calendar. The agent sends the slot to the tradie and the tenant, and either can ask for another time. Suggested new times are free for the tradie and fit the availability the tenant gave. 9. Choosing the channel: within 24 hours of a person's last message, reply on the channel they used. Otherwise send by SMS, or by email if there's no mobile number. 10. Ratings: when a job is done, the property manager rates the tradie 1–5 and the tenant is asked "Was it fixed properly?" (1–5). Both feed the tradie's myEST8 rating used in rule 5.

docs.title: Technology Implementation
docs.text:
The product has four main areas: communication management, classification, tradie recommendation, and scheduling and approvals. They're built as one app with internal modules (intake agent, tickets, quotes, scheduling, notifications), with the AI agent running as a background worker inside it, rather than as separate microservices. A team of 5 can't deploy and connect several services in 4 weeks, and module boundaries give the same separation (ADR-0001).

Only property managers have accounts. Tenants, tradies and property owners use their existing channels, apart from the no-login photo upload page (ADR-0002).

docs.title: Problem Statement V 0.1
docs.text:
Currently the version of this document is from the seminar check individual contribution for additional problem statements.

The main problem facing individual property managers is the follow up and continual re-scheduling of contractors for fixing repair issues that have arisen for current tenants. This affects the current tenants and property owners as the former needs to live with the issues for a prolonged period of time and the property owner needs to pay additional funds to complete repairs.

This needs to change as it adds additional load to the property managers administrative processes and hinders the SMB from growth in management of additional properties.

docs.title: Problem Statement V 1
docs.text:
Reframed Problem Statement

With aging buildings and lacking incentives to repair, property managers spend too much time coordinating maintainence repairs for severe repairs. It affects the small or individual property managers who spend a majority of their time on communication and matianence admin work. This process bottleneck needs to change because it reduces property managers ability to satisfy residents and gain additional properties for management.

HMW help small property managers coordinate severe building repairs with less time spent on communication and admin, so they can keep residents satisfied and take on more properties?

  1. Martin, C. et al. (June 2025). Rights at Risk: Rising Rents and Repercussions. UNSW City Futures Research Centre with the ACOSS-UNSW Sydney Poverty and Inequality Partnership, National Shelter and NARO. It is a national survey of 1,019 private renters.
    • 50% of renters live in homes needing repairs, and 10% need urgent repairs.
    • 74% had some defect or issue. The most common were pests (31%), leaks or flooding (24%), hot water problems (21%) and mould in bathrooms (18%).
    • 68% worry that asking for repairs could trigger a rent increase, and 56% fear eviction. That tension makes repair coordination harder for managers.
    • It is not Sydney-specific, and it covers tenants rather than managers' time.
  2. Aidan Devine (Sept 2025). Dirty truth behind rise of horror living conditions in rental homes. Survey of 148 landlords
    • Finder survey of 148 landlords found that two in five (38 per cent) have had a tenant wait longer than is reasonable for a repair in the last year.
Who are they?

According to the latest ABS data (as at 30 June 2026), there were 2.8 million actively trading businesses in Australia, with 996,203 of them employing staff, which means roughly 1.82 million had no employees at all. Small businesses (fewer than 20 employees) make up 97% of all actively trading businesses, or about 2.7 million, so the great majority of small businesses are non-employing sole traders or partnerships. On employment, the most recent figures show small businesses employed over 5 million people, which is 39% of the private sector workforce in 2023-24 (ASBFEO Small Business Data Portal). The standard definition for SMB is a compnay that hires 1-20 employees for "small" businesses and 21-100 for medium businesses. These businesses must also be earning revenue less than $50 million annually for small and less than $1 billion annually for medium sized businesses.

Owners Time

A large share of the owner's week goes on admin work rather than on customers or growth. A global Sage survey of over 3,000 SMBs found the average Australian business spends 81 days per year on admin tasks (vs a 120-day global average, Sage), and one summary of Xero data puts it at 10.5 hours a week, with financial admin the heaviest part. One in three owners say financial admin is their most difficult admin task, followed by marketing and sales (22%) and legal and compliance (20.3%), and chasing money is a big piece of it, since 44% of Australian small business invoices get paid late (Xero Small Business Insights). As for decisions, the structure of the sector largely answers that: with about two-thirds of small businesses having no employees (ABS) and most of the rest employing one to four people, the owner is usually the only decision-maker, so pricing, quoting, hiring, purchasing, cash flow and compliance all wait on one person (this is an inference from the business counts, not a surveyed figure). The cost shows up in what gets pushed aside: 42% of SMB leaders surveyed by Dext said they had missed business opportunities due to time lost to financial admin, and owners in an older Reckon survey reported spending more time each week on administration and payroll (10 or more hours) than operating at their peak (fewer than 10 hours).

Therefore the main goal for the designed product is to assist in growth despite the admin work requirement This means either being able to distribute the owner's decision making to multipler areas (Stream 1), lessen the admin work requirement (Stream 2), or train the work force for AI adoption for a more efficient process (Stream 3).

SMB AI Usage

At the strict end, the ABS found about 12 per cent of Australian businesses used AI in 2024–25, falling to around 11 per cent for small and micro businesses. Broader surveys come in much higher: NAB research puts active AI use at 42% of SMEs, with another 14% planning to adopt, the National AI Centre's tracker recorded 44% in February 2026, an Intuit QuickBooks survey found regular use reached 69% in January 2026, and auDA's Digital Lives of Australians 2026 found 72% of small businesses had used AI (via SEO Summer). The tools are mostly general-purpose assistants and features built into software they already use, ranging from free chatbots to agentic AI tools, applied to routine work: data processing (38%), administration (36%), marketing (34%), customer service (32%), and bookkeeping (32%) (Intuit QuickBooks). NAB respondents most often named automating admin tasks as the main benefit (64%), and Xero data (via Melbourne AI Agents) suggests a third of small businesses using AI save 11 to 20 staff hours a month. The evidence points more to stalling than quitting: Waymouth Tech notes that most SMBs use off-the-shelf assistants for writing and summarising while far fewer have AI built into core workflows, only 12% of Intuit's respondents call AI core to their operations, and the National AI Centre tracker dipped from 45% to 43% between quarters. Waymouth also lists open-ended chatbots, vague "AI strategy" projects and over-ambitious agent systems as the uses most likely to underperform. Both sources you supplied are AI consultancies, so they have a commercial interest in the topic; the Melbourne AI Agents page is mostly a roundup of NAB, MYOB, Xero, Deloitte and ABS figures, and the Waymouth piece is largely commentary rather than new data.

The upside of closing the gap is large. Deloitte Access Economics models that wider SMB AI adoption could add $44 billion to the economy and lift profitability by 45–111%, MYOB data shows SMEs using AI products growing 2.8× faster than non-users, and the Tech Council of Australia and Microsoft estimate generative AI could contribute $115 billion a year by 2030.

AI Usage Blockers

The main blocker for AI usage depends on the market, and on whether the business has tried AI yet. The surveys split into two groups that report different problems:

Who is asked Top blocker Figure Source SMEs not using AI Distrust of AI decision-making / want to keep human control ~65% National AI Centre, Dec 2025 – Feb 2026 SMEs not using AI "AI is not relevant to my business" 54% National AI Centre, Dec 2025 – Feb 2026 All SMEs "Don't know how to use AI in my business" 19% National AI Centre, Dec 2025 – Feb 2026 SMBs using or considering AI Privacy and security 39% (higher than US 36%, UK 35%) Intuit QuickBooks 2026 Impact Report SMBs using or considering AI Fear of failure / making mistakes 39% Intuit QuickBooks 2026 Impact Report SMBs using or considering AI Not knowing what AI can do 31% Intuit QuickBooks 2026 Impact Report All businesses (ICT generally) Insufficient staff skills 16% ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business 2024–25 All businesses (ICT generally) Uncertain cost/benefit 13% ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business 2024–25 Mid-sized businesses (20–500 staff) AI tools not connected to other systems only 23% connected Decidr, State of AI in Australian Business 2026

What comes up most: for businesses that haven't started, it is trust and relevance rather than cost. Two in three non-adopters would rather keep a human in control, and more than half don't see how AI applies to their work. For businesses already using AI, the blocker moves to privacy and confidence (privacy 39%, fear of getting it wrong 39%, not knowing what it can do 31%), the same three barriers Accountants Daily highlights. Cost comes up less than you'd expect. The ABS barriers that mention money (cost/benefit uncertainty 13%, lack of funds 15% for innovation) sit below skills and time; and when the ABS asked about barriers to collaboration, insufficient time (26%) was the top answer.

Stalling vs stopping: No reliable Australian figure was found for businesses that tried AI and then stopped. What the data does show is stalling at shallow use: - Only 12% of Intuit's respondents call AI core to their operations, even though 69% use it regularly. - Employment Hero's SME Pulse (Apr–Jun 2026, 600 leaders) found only 13% of micro businesses use AI company-wide; 37% describe their use as "limited", 22% are not using it in any meaningful way, and 25% have no AI investment at all. (Employment Hero defines micro as fewer than 21 staff, which is different from the ABS definition.) - The National AI Centre tracker dipped from 45% to 43% between quarters. - COSBOA has warned that 2.7 million small businesses need support to see a payoff from AI (Small Business Connections).

Blockers are different by sector. The tracker splits sectors: construction and agriculture are below 30% adoption, while health, education and services are above 50%. An earlier quarter put construction at 34% adopting and 25% not aware of how to use AI (National AI Centre, 2024 Q4). The ABS figures show a similar split (construction 6%, info media & telco 38%). This is why the next section looks at where the gap is largest.

docs.title: High Potential Markets
docs.text:
"High potential" here means lots of businesses × low current AI use × a heavy admin load that AI is already good at (quoting, invoicing, scheduling, bookkeeping). The ABS Business Characteristics Survey gives the strictest AI-use figures by industry. Business counts are from ABS Counts of Australian Businesses, with the construction count via Money.com.au (June 2025):

Industry AI use 2024–25 (ABS BCS) Number of businesses Notes Information media & telecommunications 38% — Highest adopter Professional, scientific & technical 24% — Already ahead Financial & insurance services 24% 139,417 (Jun 2026) Grew 24× since 2021–22 Health care & social assistance 17% 227,702 (Jun 2026) NAIC tracker: >50% Retail trade 9% — Construction 6% 462,939 (Jun 2025) — largest industry, ~17% of all businesses NAIC tracker: <30% Accommodation & food services 5% — Low use, but fewer businesses Agriculture, forestry & fishing 3% 170,185 (Jun 2026) Very low use, but ~⅓ the size of construction Transport, postal & warehousing 1% 261,109 (Jun 2026) Lowest use of all

The largest AI adoption gap in the market is construction trades. Construction is Australia's biggest industry by business count (Money.com.au), yet only about 6% of construction businesses reported using AI (half the 12% national rate) (ABS). The government tracker agrees, with construction under 30% against more than 50% in health and services. Agriculture and transport have lower rates, but they have far fewer businesses (170k and 261k compared with 463k). Construction also carries the most financial distress: it made up 27% of all companies entering external administration in 2023–24 (2,975 companies, ASIC).

The sector is almost entirely small. About 98.5% of construction firms have fewer than 20 employees and 91% have fewer than 5 (Builders Institute, citing ABS/CEDA, June 2024). Most of these are construction services, meaning the trades: plumbing, electrical, carpentry, tiling and plastering.

However, the biggest opportunity area for AI is the agricultural sector. Agriculture, forestry and fishing has 170,185 businesses. The number shrank 0.5% in 2025–26, while total business numbers grew (ABS, Counts of Australian Businesses). Only 3% of agriculture businesses used AI in 2024–25, a quarter of the 12% national rate (ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business 2024–25). Even on the National AI Centre's broader measure, agriculture sits below 30%, compared with over 50% in health and services (National AI Centre). This isn't because farmers avoid technology: 72% already use agtech such as farm management software, electronic ID tags and satellite tools (Roy Morgan, 2024).

Not only are these farms facing a severe ageing problem among owners and workers, but skilled farm labour is also in short supply. Ageing: Agriculture has the oldest owner-operators of any industry, and their median age rose from 51 to 56 between 2001 and 2016 (ABARES, Agricultural workforce trends). Livestock farmers now have a median age of 62, compared with 39 across all occupations, and 34.6% are 65 or older (Jobs and Skills Australia, Livestock Farmers). The workforce behind them is shrinking: industry employment fell by 7,900 (–2.6%) in the year to February 2026, and the median worker is 51 (Jobs and Skills Australia, Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing). Skills: 57% of horticulture farms had difficulty recruiting in 2021–22 (ABARES, Labour use 2021–22), and 34% still did in 2022–23 (ABARES via ARR News). Only about 37% of livestock farm workers hold a Certificate III or higher (Jobs and Skills Australia, Livestock Farm Workers). Farms also keep taking on workers with no farm-specific knowledge. 64% of contract horticulture workers now come through labour hire (ABARES via ARR News), and the PALM scheme, a major source of seasonal farm labour, had 28,535 workers in December 2025 (PALM scheme data).

The main barriers to adoption in this industry are price and perceived relevance. Cost is the top barrier to new farm technology (66%), 23% of farmers see no need for it, and 19% see little benefit (Roy Morgan, 2024). Across all SMEs, 54% of businesses not using AI say it isn't relevant to them (National AI Centre). Lack of knowledge (37%) and poor connectivity (36%) also rank highly (Roy Morgan, 2024). Trusted advice is hard to reach, too. Farmers rely most on other farmers, farm consultants and input suppliers. Only 27% trust government agriculture departments and 19% trust banks (QARS 2023–24 via Farm Online).

Real Estate Management is also an area of opportunity given the wide array of workers. Property managers coordinate landlords, tenants, tradespeople and strata. They help 1 in 3 Australians into homes (MRI Software, 2024) and manage about 90% of investment properties (REIQ). The rental, hiring and real estate services industry employs 235,200 people, 157,000 of them in real estate services (Jobs and Skills Australia, Rental, Hiring and Real Estate Services). The workforce is under strain. 29% of property managers intend to leave the profession, up from 13% in 2018. 66% say their workload is busy or far too busy, and 47% work more than 41 hours a week (Real Estate Business, MRI Voice of the Property Manager 2024). 54% report mental health struggles (MRI Software, 2024). Unlike agriculture, the gap here is in how deeply AI is used, not whether it's used at all. 11% of rental, hiring and real estate businesses use AI, close to the 12% national rate (ABS, Characteristics of Australian Business 2024–25). 55% of property organisations use AI, but only 18% say their AI capability is "stable and growing", and internal skills are the top barrier (28%) (Real Estate Business, Yardi & Property Council 2026). Property managers are open to it: 72% see AI as a significant opportunity to improve productivity and work-life balance (MRI Software, 2024).

**Currently, the sector of choice is Real Estate Management **

docs.title: Team Meeting: 30/09 (Week 3)
docs.text:
Problem Statement v0.1

Property managers spend excessive time chasing and rescheduling contractors for tenant repairs, so repairs drag on. Tenants live with unresolved issues and owners pay more from delays and repeat visits. This admin load caps manager capacity and stops small and mid-sized agencies from taking on more properties.

Key insights

  • People resist changing how they work, so managing adoption matters as much as the tool.
  • If a question only has 1–2 possible answers, the problem statement is too narrow.
  • Some trades businesses run without the owner present. How is the owner's knowledge handed over to workers?
  • Tenant screening is manual: rental history, bank statements, payslips, ID, tenancy database, pets, cars and a phone interview, plus emailing the previous agent.
  • Customer churn is agencies' top concern. AI could help them keep up with legal changes.
  • A government-sponsored AI bot carries more trust than a general tool like ChatGPT.
  • Advertising, open houses, inspections and travel between properties all take time, and tribunal disputes add prep work.

5 Whys by issue

Issue Root cause found Evidence Contractor coordination (maintenance) Managers rely on small personal tradie lists because there is no trusted, shared contractor directory. Quality is passed by word of mouth, and tradie data (availability, capacity, past jobs) isn't digitised, so AI has nothing to match on. PropertyChat, REIQ, Climate Control News, ServiceTitan 2025 (43% use basic tools or paper, 70% get work by referral) End-of-lease damage claims The 14-day tribunal window forces claims to the top of the queue, and most repair and bond claims arrive at lease end. Team discussion Poor repair quality Owners push managers to keep repair costs low, so contractors deliver low-quality work. Macquarie 2023 Tenant screening Vacancy days are a measured KPI but damage isn't traced back to screening, so managers rush slow, error-prone reference checks. Team discussion Tenant request overload Requests arrive through many channels and agents manually track, prioritise and follow up with tenants, owners and contractors. Team discussion

Who cares

  • Actors: tenant (requests repair), property manager (coordinates), contractor (does the work)
  • Stakeholders: landlord/owner/strata, prospective tenants
  • Beneficiaries: contractors billed by the hour

The problem is complicated: solving it needs property managers' expertise on practical coordination issues and on what data a solution would need.

Reframes

  1. Shift the category: if contractors fail to meet standard, how might we help property managers verify contractor work quality and expand beyond their personal list?
  2. Zoom out: if owner buy-in is the blocker, how might we help property managers secure owner approval and budget sign-off through cost optimisation?
  3. Challenge the goal: if contractors don't want small-agency jobs, how might we make those jobs worth prioritising?

Success looks like: managers coordinate maintenance with suitable contractors faster and more easily. Owners are kept updated and spend less on repairs. Tenants are more satisfied and churn less.

Action items

  • Each teammate finds 2 businesses to interview: are they using AI and for what, and what is holding them back from growing?
  • Verify the key issues (maintenance, tenant screening, tribunal disputes) with them.

docs.title: UAT Testing
docs.text:
User Acceptance Testing (UAT) checks with real Property Managers whether myEST8 supports how a small Sydney Agency actually handles maintenance, whether its wording makes sense, and whether anything important is missing before the final presentation.

Status: planned. Sessions run 5–9 November 2026.

The test plan and scenarios below are final. The Results section is filled in from the UAT pack (myEST8_UAT_Pack.xlsx) after the sessions.

docs.title: Test plan
docs.text: Item Detail Objective Validate that a Property Manager at a small Agency can run the full maintenance workflow in myEST8, from a Tenant's first message to a finished Job, and that the product fits their day-to-day work. Where https://myest8.vercel.app, the current production build from master. Desktop browser (Chrome, Edge or Safari) at 1366–1440 px, plus the tester's own phone for one scenario. When Thursday 5 and Friday 6 November, the weekend of 7–8 November, and Monday 9 November as a fallback. In person or over Zoom/Teams, about 50 minutes each. Who Tester: a practising Property Manager at a small Agency. Facilitator: runs the session and plays the Tenant, Tradie and Property Owner from test phones and inboxes. Note-taker: fills in the UAT pack live. Product owner: triages defects and signs off. In scope Sign-up and onboarding; adding Properties, Tenants, Owners and Tradies (one by one and by import); Tenant reporting by SMS and email; follow-up questions and photo upload; the AI-filled Summary, Trade and Urgency; confirming a Maintenance Request; Urgent Repairs; Quote Requests, Estimates, Site Inspections and Firm Quotes; Owner approval; Work Orders and visit booking; the Tenant progress page; Dashboard, Dispatch, Tickets, Archive, Approvals, Schedule, Profiles and Settings. Out of scope Billing, trust accounting and rent; PropertyMe or Console Cloud integration; load and security testing; native apps; per-Agency WhatsApp numbers; Common Area repairs beyond passing them to the Building Manager. Test data Agency "Harbourside Rentals (UAT)". Properties 12 King St, Newtown (Max Repair Cost $500) and 4/18 Wattle St, Ultimo ($300). Tenant Priya Shah, Owner Daniel Ng, Tradies Drip Doctors, Flow Bros Plumbing (Nominated for King St) and Sparkright Electrical. All made up. No tester's own tenants, owners or tradies are ever contacted. Session outline 5 min welcome and consent → 35 min scenarios, thinking aloud → 5 min SUS questionnaire and open questions → 5 min wrap-up

docs.title: Entry and exit criteria
docs.text:
Entry: the production deploy is green (CI deploy-prod and smoke passed); the test Agency, phones and inboxes are ready; the tester has read the information sheet and consented.

Exit (all must be met to accept):

  1. Every High-priority scenario has been run by at least 3 testers.
  2. No open Critical defects.
  3. No more than 2 open High defects, each with a planned fix.
  4. Average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 68 or more, the commonly cited industry average (Brooke 1996; Sauro 2011).
  5. The team has reviewed all feedback.

docs.title: Severity and status definitions
docs.text:
Severity Meaning Critical Data loss, the wrong person contacted, or the flow can't continue High A main task is wrong or confusing with no workaround Medium Wrong or confusing, but there is a workaround Low Cosmetic, wording or layout

Status values: Pass (behaved as expected), Fail (didn't; log a defect), Blocked (couldn't be run because of an earlier failure or missing setup), Not run.

Defect handling: each failure gets one row in the defect log, linked to its scenario. The team triages daily during the UAT window. Fixes go through the normal PR into dev, then a release to master, and are retested in the next session.
